attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post. He states it as fact ("That much is true").

semantics.note: The proposition states the cumulative observation as of publication accurately. The text adds "AI" to "big companies", which the context supports.

contract.note: Reading "big companies" as the providers the post names (Google, OpenAI, Anthropic), checked against Amazon, is an ordinary reading. Counting betas and previews as "introduced" matches Marcus's own text, which notes Astra is only in beta.

evidence.note: OpenAI system card dated 2025-07-17 introduces ChatGPT agent, before the post. Company disclosure of its own launch.
Anthropic put computer use into public API beta on 2024-10-22: an action-taking capability introduced before the cutoff.
Google introduced the Project Mariner agent prototype to trusted testers on 2024-12-11, which counts as an introduction under the contract.
Amazon released a Nova Act research preview for building browser agents on 2025-03-31, which corroborates the claim beyond the named firms.

reviews.rationale: Dated primary disclosures show that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Amazon had all introduced agents or agent capabilities before 2025-08-03. The packet contains no counterevidence of a major provider without one. The claim is supported under the contract's fair reading of "big companies" and "introduced".

attribution.note: Marcus's own assessment in his post, following a quoted OpenAI caveat.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the causal link (errors limited utility), the magnitude ("greatly") and the ChatGPT agent example.

contract.note: The plain reading (substantially reduced usable completion, or a heavy correction burden) is ordinary. It does not require errors to be the only cause. Limiting the check to ChatGPT agent's first weeks matches the post.

evidence.note: A hands-on test (dated 2025-07-30) ties failed or inaccurate outputs to unusable results on several tasks. It is a single user, and it does not measure the overall magnitude.
A Tom's Guide test (2025-07-28) found real usefulness, with occasional need to step in. It covers selected tasks and does not measure losses caused by errors.

reviews.rationale: Two anecdotal reviews point in different directions: one finds frequent failures, the other substantial usefulness. Neither gives representative measurements that separate error effects from crashes, access limits or approval steps. The evidence cannot establish whether errors "greatly" limited utility.

attribution.note: Marcus's own forward-looking statement in his post.

semantics.note: "I don't expect ... will be" is unhedged expectation, so it is a scored forecast. The proposition keeps "eventually" and the superlative scale.

contract.note: An open horizon with an early-contradiction rule (agents broadly abandoned) is fair. The plain reading of the scale comparison is ordinary.

evidence.note: St. Louis Fed data on generative AI in general, from before the forecast. It is not about agents and cannot settle a forecast with no deadline.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline ("eventually"), and nothing in the packet meets the early-resolution rule. Agents have not been abandoned, and their time savings have not been measured at historic scale. The only evidence is pre-forecast context about generative AI broadly, so the claim cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own framing line, introducing an embedded example in his agents post.

semantics.note: The post's context limits the claim to AI agents. The proposition carries over "frequently" without adding a rate.

contract.note: Taking 2025 up to the post date as the period, and reading "frequently" as recurring and well documented across systems, is ordinary and fair.

evidence.note: Anthropic's Project Vend report (published 2025-06-27) documents several hallucinations by its shop-running agent in March–April 2025.
Ars Technica (2025-07-24) reports confabulation by the Gemini CLI and Replit agents in July 2025.

reviews.rationale: Documented 2025 cases show agents from Anthropic, Google and Replit fabricating people, meetings, file operations and data before the post date. The packet has no evidence that fabrication was rare. Under the contract's reading of "frequently" as recurring across systems, the claim is supported.
